messages.body_plain:
scanone compares a single QTL model to the null model.
In addqtl, you have some base model M, and you compare M to M + {Q}.

I recommend using the same threshold as from scanone. See chapter 9 of the R/qtl book, http://rqtl.org/book

karl

messages.subject: Re: QTL detection
messages.body_plain:
I ignore those p-values columns, as they don't account for the search across locus pairs.

I recommend doing a permutation test, though it's extremely computationally intensive.

As an approximation, you could use a Bonferroni adjustment of the nominal p-values: multiply them by the number of locus pairs you've considered.

See also chapter 8 of the R/qtl book, http://rqtl.org/book

karl

messages.body_plain:
>
> First i would like to know if its possible to replace the indiviudals name from an integer to a string.
> By default each individual of a mapping population is given a number from 1 to nth individual.
> When transfering the cross object to ASMap package, it would be nice to have actual names of the individuals.

Individual IDs are taken as a phenotype called "id". So you could change that column, or add it to your data file.

   mycross$pheno$id <- [some vector of names]

> Second issue is reading in phenotypic data. I am testing different large maps and wanted to know if its possible to add phenotypic data directly to the cross object
> without having to add them to the genotypic data and reload the whole file.

You can plug in any other data frame into as the "pheno" component of the cross object. You just want to make sure the individuals are in the same order as in the genotype data.

  mycross$pheno <- [some other data frame]

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Arbitrary distances for no marker positions
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Arbitrary distances for no marker positions
messages.body_plain:
For QTL analysis, R/qtl generally needs ordered markers with an estimated genetic map.

If no marker positions are provided, in reading in the data the markers are assigned positions on a grid with a fixed distance between markers.

In the scanone() analysis results you show, positions like "c1B.loc122" are "pseudomarker" positions that are selected according to the step size used in the call to calc.genoprob or sim.geno. But if the markers are not ordered and their positions are not known, it would be best to restrict analysis to the typed markers (which is accomplished with step=0). But I'd recommend against this, too, because treatment of any missing genotypes is done using information on all markers on each chromosome, which would not be meaningful if the markers are not ordered and their genetic map positions known.

It's best to first seek to construct a genetic map for the markers.

karl

I'm using GigaMUGA data that comes as text files, including a Sample_Map file and FinalReport file (the FinalReport file is large at 143,259 SNPs by 96 samples). These files are combined with a GigaMUGA SNPS file that are run through the argyle program for R. From there the data goes into R/qtl. I'm not as familiar with the LMM (Linear Mixed Models) approach. I've already done scanone and am trying to figure out the MQM or scantwo for the data. My collaborators already have a gene of interest and are hoping to find a modifier or something else that works in conjunction with their known and fixed gene of interest. The QTL corresponding to the gene of interest does seem to be popping up on the scanone runs. Now I'm hoping to give them another QTL to investigate for their model.
Thanks for the help.
Bill

On Friday, August 26, 2016 at 8:04:35 PM UTC-4, pjotrp wrote:

> On Thu, Aug 25, 2016 at 11:48:11AM -0700, william...@cchmc.org wrote:
> > I'm having a similar error, the "singular matrix" error. I also had the "Some markers at the same position" error. I assume this is the map problem that Danny was talking about. I'm trying to follow his recommendation, but I'm using GigaMUGA data for my analysis. I started with 143,259 SNPs (the whole set) and dwindled it down to  31,642 SNPs that are informative between the two mouse strains of interest. Is this data set too big? I seem to have problem markers on every chromosome and haven't been able to fix them yet. I'm guessing this will be a big job. Any help is appreciated.
> > Thanks
>
> If your data is in VCF format you can use my bio-vcf to apply sensible
> filters to this data. I have an example of an approach with GTEx here:
>
>   https://github.com/pjotrp/bioruby-vcf/blob/master/doc/GTEx_reduce.md
>
> It may also be interesting to use an LMM on your data - in addition to
> scanone and MQM. Karl has an implementation in R/qtl2, and we have one
> on http://genenetwork.org/ (use Genenetwork 2 to try pylmm).
>
> Pjotr Prins
